assertions.text: exception where individually represented by counsel
applies to an employee who primarily works in California
assertions.note: sources state the test is an employee who primarily works AND RESIDES in California. The clause states only 'works', which overstates the section's reach — an employee working in California but residing elsewhere may fall outside it.

gaps: The prohibition attaches to requiring the provision as a condition of employment. The clause omits that qualifier and reads as though any such provision is voidable however it arose.
Injunctive relief is available alongside fees. The clause mentions only fees.

judicialQuotations.case: Zhang v. Super. Ct. (Cal. Ct. App. 2022)
judicialQuotations.quote: Labor Code section 925 provides in part: "(a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: [¶] (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California."

judicialQuotations.case: Midwest Motor Supply Co. v. Super. Ct. (Cal. Ct. App. 2020)
judicialQuotations.quote: Section 925 provides: "An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would . . . :[¶] (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California." (§ 925, subd. (a).) "Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is voidable by the employee..."

judicialNote: Two California Courts of Appeal, two years apart, quote §925(a) verbatim and both give the test as "primarily resides AND works in California". The clause says "primarily works", dropping the residence conjunct. This is independent corroboration of exactly the kind that was missing: two courts, not two summaries of one summary. It is still read through CourtListener, which republishes the opinions rather than issuing them, so the two-primary standard is not met — what has changed is that the claim is no longer unverifiable as recorded.
